summary: We developed a visual tool that renders 5 variables (temperature, rainfall, snowfall, surface pressure and wind speed) onto a globe and 2D projection. The data spans monthly from 2000 - present and only considers land data excluding Antarctica. Our data is then put through a series of statistical tests to highlight the significance of any trends that appear on local or larger geographic scales. We also included a 6 month forecast by extrapolating from previous anomalous (different from predictions) data points and extending these "anomalous differences" to the future predicted model. All of this can be used to predict patterns in the lengths and severity of storm seasons which is of very broad social importance, especially in developing countries with less infrastructure in place to handle the effects. Our focus is on the effect this may have on strong and stable internet connections, which, as the modern world is progressing, is gaining more and more significance. Storms have the effect of both physically damaging mobile masts and impeding the broadcast signal due to absorption of the microwaves by water so predicting when and how long they occur for is crucial for internet service providers to be able to have rigorous plans in place for the roll-out and maintenance of infrastructure.
details:
Our tool renders a 3D globe with gridpoints along with a smaller 2D projection without gridpoints. A menu of 5 variables (using data collected from FLDAS Noah Land Surface Model) including temperature, surface pressure, rainfall, snowfall and wind speed selects which variable is displayed on the maps. A slider can then be used to see the data evolve over time, displaying the raw data for each month, from January 2000 to September 2026, on the gridpoints of the globe and regionally on the 2D projection. This slider can be selected to automatically scroll showing the evolution of the selected variable over time. On the globe, only the data points within a certain radius of the cursor are shown at any given point so as to make the viewing experience easier for the user, though the 2D projection renders all of the data to act as a reference for the more precise globe. Upon zooming into a region, selecting a gridpoint with the cursor will display the coordinates of that gridpoint, the time series for the selected variable at that location over the full dataset, rates of change of each variable along with some other calculations and, importantly, the values for a series of statistical tests: Hamed-Rao, Newey-West estimator (HAC-p) and Theil-Sen estimator (sen's slope). At the end of this time series, a forecast for 6 months into the future of our dataset can be found, calculated by analysing the anomalous data points already in the data set and extrapolating that to a future model with Nino 4 data.

This very visual approach lends itself to displaying highly resolved data in an easy to understand way with an easy route to get all of the information required for analysis.

Our project is intended to be used primarily by analysts due to the technical nature of the information we supply, but can also be used by anyone with an interest in seeing how the world evolves over time due to the simplicity of the UI.

HTML, Python and CSS were used on Idle and VScode software. Claude was used as a tool to aid in the writing of sections of the code.

Our ideas stemmed from wanting to provide a comfortable user experience, leading to the separated globe and 2D projections as well as the radial rendering of the data around the cursor.

We considered our target audience and a unique interface as the building blocks of the project, allowing for simple data visualisation where accessing the data can be very challenging, especially for the inexperienced.
dataRefs: FLDAS Noah Land Surface Model L4 Global Monthly 0.1 x 0.1 degree (MERRA-2 and CHIRPS) (FLDAS_NOAH01_C_GL_M)
Niño 4 SST Index from the NOAA ERSST V6
